title: The FRONTIER Act
description: A close reading of H.R. 9925 (July 2026): who it covers, what it requires, emergency orders and the fight over preemption.
caveat: Based on the introduced text of H.R. 9925 (July 23, 2026). Status, cosponsors and reactions checked October 19, 2026. Simplified: check the bill text before relying on details. The bill could change in committee.

units.title: Meet the bill
units.desc: Who wrote it, what it targets, and where it stands.

items.p: Who are the lead sponsors of the FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)?
o: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA)
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN)
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT)
Rep. Don Beyer (D-VA) and Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI)
items.x: Obernolte introduced it on July 23, 2026, with Trahan as an original cosponsor. Cruz and Klobuchar had been negotiating a separate Senate draft, but those talks stalled on September 29, 2026; Hawley and Blumenthal wrote a different bill that would have the Department of Energy evaluate models.

items.p: Which House committees was it referred to?
o: Energy and Commerce; Science, Space, and Technology
Judiciary only
Armed Services, plus the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
Ways and Means, plus Financial Services and Small Business
items.x: Energy and Commerce oversees the Commerce Department, which would run the new rules. As of October 19, 2026, congress.gov listed no committee action since the July 23 referral, so neither committee had held a markup.

items.p: As of mid-October 2026, what does the bill's cosponsor list look like?
o: 11: 6 Democrats and 5 Republicans
More than 100, mostly Republicans
Only one: Rep. Trahan, the lead Democrat
About 40, almost all of them Democrats
items.x: Five original cosponsors joined on July 23, and six more signed on between September 16 and October 1 (congress.gov, checked October 19, 2026). Several groups quoted in a July 28 release from Rep. Trahan's office praised it; the AI Verification & Evaluation Research Institute called it "the strongest federal proposal to date."

items.p: What is the bill mainly trying to prevent?
o: Catastrophic harms from the most powerful AI models
Bias in hiring algorithms
Deepfakes in political ads
Chatbots giving bad financial advice
items.x: It covers only frontier models and defines its target narrowly: catastrophic risks such as AI help with weapons of mass destruction, autonomous cyberattacks and models evading human control. Everyday AI harms are left to other laws, including state laws.

items.p: Which agency would run the new rules?
o: The Commerce Department, via a new Under Secretary for AI Security
A new independent AI agency led by a bipartisan commission
The Department of Energy, through its national labs
The Federal Trade Commission, through a new AI bureau
items.x: The bill creates an Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security to write rules, license auditors and receive reports. The Secretary of Commerce keeps the power to issue emergency orders.

items.p: What makes an AI model a "frontier model" under the bill?
o: It's a foundation model trained with over 10^26 operations
It has more than 1 billion monthly users worldwide
It can pass the bar exam and other expert-level tests
Its developer has more than 500 full-time employees
items.x: The bill uses a compute threshold: more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. That's roughly the scale of the largest training runs, so only a handful of companies' models qualify.

items.p: A lab fine-tunes its own model that was trained with slightly under 10^26 operations, pushing the total over the line. Is the result a frontier model?
o: Yes. Fine-tuning compute counts toward the total
No. Only the original pre-training run counts toward the threshold
It depends on whether the fine-tuning run by itself exceeds 10^26 operations
It becomes one when the model is released to the public
items.x: The definition counts compute for the original training run plus any later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or other substantial modification. That closes the gap of training a model just under the line and topping it up later.

items.p: Under the bill's definition, how big does a single incident have to be to count as "catastrophic"?
o: Over 50 deaths or serious injuries, or over $1 billion in property damage
Any death or serious injury the model contributes to, however few people are hurt
More than $100 million in losses
Death or serious injury to more than 1,000 people, or over $10 billion in property damage
items.x: Those thresholds come from the definition of catastrophic risk. The harm also has to come from specific kinds of model behavior, such as weapons help or acting without human oversight.

items.p: Match each pathway in the bill's definition of catastrophic risk to an example.
pairs: Giving non-public help building a chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or cyber weapon
Carrying out a cyberattack or theft with no meaningful human oversight
Evading control of its developer or user
items.x: A risk only counts if it's foreseeable and material and could cause harm at the scale of more than 50 deaths or $1 billion in a single incident.

items.p: What kind of model behavior does the bill explicitly carve out of its definition of catastrophic risk?
o: A model repeating information that's already publicly available elsewhere
A model giving step-by-step help designing a bioweapon
A model stealing money on its own, with no human directing it
A model hiding what it can do from its developer's monitoring
items.x: The definition carves out outputs that are publicly accessible in substantially similar form from a non-AI source, lawful federal government activity, and harms where the model didn't materially contribute.

units.title: Three tiers
units.desc: Duties grow with the developer's size.

items.p: Match each tier to its definition.
pairs: Has trained, or started training, a model above 10^26 operations
Over $50 million in revenue and at least $1 billion in AI spending over 36 months
Over $5 billion in revenue and at least $10 billion in AI spending over 36 months
items.x: Revenue and spending are measured over the preceding 36 months and include affiliates. Both tests must be met for the bigger tiers.

items.p: Why does the bill require both a revenue test and an AI-spending test for the bigger tiers?
o: So the heaviest duties fall only on big companies spending heavily on frontier AI
So any company with little revenue still gets the heaviest duties if it trains a frontier model
Because the Constitution requires two tests
To exempt every lab from all duties until it turns a profit
items.x: Both tests must be met, so a big company that trains one frontier model but spends little on AI stays in the lowest tier, and so does a lab with little revenue. The lowest tier has no revenue test at all, so even a revenue-free lab over the compute line still owes transparency and incident reports.

items.p: A very large frontier developer has to follow which rules?
o: The rules of all three tiers
Only the very large tier's rules
Only the rules it chooses to opt into
None until an auditor is licensed
items.x: Section 6 makes the obligations cumulative: each tier carries the duties of the tiers below it.

items.p: Can the Under Secretary change the 10^26 compute threshold or the dollar thresholds?
o: Only upward, by regulation, with regular reviews
Yes, up or down at any time
No, only Congress can change them, by passing a new law
Only the President can, by issuing an executive order
items.x: The bill lets the Under Secretary raise the thresholds as algorithms, hardware and costs change, but not lower them. Daniel King, a Foundation for American Innovation research fellow who praised the bill, argued the compute threshold should also be able to move down, since algorithmic gains could let smaller training runs reach the same capabilities.

items.p: Match each duty to who has to do it.
pairs: Every frontier developer, before or when it deploys a model
Every frontier developer, within 72 hours of an incident
items.x: The design puts light, cheap duties on everyone over the compute line and saves the expensive outside verification for the few biggest labs.

items.p: About how many companies are expected to face the top-tier independent verification requirement?
o: A handful, roughly five
Hundreds
Every company that uses AI
None, because it's voluntary
items.x: Dan Parshall of the Canary Institute estimates the top tier is "roughly five companies." He presents this as a gap: emergency orders can reach any frontier developer, but the only required early warning, an IVO's duty to refer imminent risks, covers just those five.

items.p: Before a large frontier developer can develop, deploy or operate a frontier model, what does it have to file with the Under Secretary?
o: A disclosure statement and a fee
A license application approved by Congress
A copy of its model weights for government safekeeping
Nothing
items.x: Registration starts one year after enactment (or 90 days after a developer qualifies, if later). Privately held developers list anyone owning 5 percent or more now or in the past 5 years. Operating without a current statement costs $10,000 a day.

units.title: Transparency and reporting
units.desc: What developers have to publish and report.

items.p: What is a "frontier AI framework"?
o: A developer's documented protocols for managing catastrophic risks
A federal technical standard that every frontier model must meet before release
A list of banned AI uses
A binding contract between a lab and the government setting its safety duties
items.x: Large frontier developers must write, follow and publish one. It has to explain their risk thresholds, how they decide whether to deploy or use a model internally, how they secure model weights and how they respond to incidents. The Under Secretary sets minimum requirements by regulation.

items.p: The annual compliance audit for large frontier developers checks what?
o: Whether the developer followed its own published framework
Whether the framework is good enough to prevent catastrophe
Whether the model passes tests run by government evaluators before release
Whether the developer's revenue still puts it in the large tier
items.x: It's a compliance check against the lab's own rules. Judging whether those rules are adequate is the job of the independent verification organizations, and only for the very largest developers. Daniel King, a Foundation for American Innovation research fellow who praised the bill, flagged this gap: for large developers, "the merits of that framework are not finely evaluated."

items.p: What does the bill ban in the relationship between a developer and its auditor?
o: Tying the auditor's pay to the audit's results
Paying the auditor at all
Letting the auditor see unredacted internal materials
Using the same auditor two years in a row
items.x: The developer may pay the auditor but can't make payment depend on the findings, and neither side may have a financial interest in the other.

items.p: When a large frontier developer makes a material change to its framework, what must it do?
o: Publish a justification within 30 days
Get the Under Secretary's written approval first
Nothing until the annual review comes around
Notify Congress
items.x: Developers review their frameworks at least annually. A significant change triggers a public explanation within 30 days, so outsiders can see when safety commitments loosen.

items.p: Match each deadline to the duty.
pairs: Tell law enforcement about an incident posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury
Report a critical safety incident to the Under Secretary
Large developers send summaries of catastrophic risk from internal use
Publish a redacted audit report and summary
items.x: The fastest deadline is for emergencies involving physical danger. Routine reporting runs on longer timelines.

items.p: What kind of event counts as a "critical safety incident" under the bill?
o: A model deceiving its developer to evade monitoring, outside a test meant to provoke it
A model deceiving its evaluators during a red-team test built to provoke that behavior
A model giving one user dangerously wrong medical advice in a chat
A data center outage that takes the model offline for a day
items.x: The definition lists four things: theft or tampering with model weights, harm from a catastrophic risk, loss of control of a model, and deceptive behavior that subverts the developer's controls in a way that shows materially higher catastrophic risk.

items.p: A lab releases a new frontier model. When must it publish its transparency report?
o: Before or at the same time as deployment
Within one year after the model is first deployed
Within 90 days after deployment
Before the model's training run begins
items.x: Every frontier developer publishes a report covering the model's intended uses, restrictions, catastrophic-risk assessments and results, and how much third parties were involved. Summaries must be machine-readable. A confidential deployment for national security can delay publication if the report goes to the Under Secretary.

items.p: What's the maximum civil penalty for violating the transparency and reporting rules?
o: $1 million per violation, with each day a separate violation
$10,000 total, no matter how many violations
$100 million per violation, plus a share of revenue
There's no penalty, only a public warning
items.x: The U.S. Attorney General can sue. State attorneys general who opt in can also sue after notifying federal officials; the Attorney General can join the case or file its own, which pauses the state's suit.

items.p: Who can see incident reports filed with the Under Secretary?
o: Only federal staff who need to know, plus state attorneys general who opt in
Anyone, through a searchable public database on the Commerce website
Only the developer that filed them
Only members of Congress, in closed session
items.x: Reports stay confidential. Each year the Under Secretary sends Congress and the President an anonymized, aggregated report, the first due by January 1, 2028. Members of the public can also file incident reports through the same confidential channel.

units.title: Independent verification
units.desc: Licensed outside reviewers for the biggest labs.

items.p: What does an independent verification organization (IVO) judge that a regular compliance auditor doesn't?
o: Whether the developer's safeguards are adequate
Whether the developer followed its own framework as written
Whether the model's financial projections are accurate
Whether the model's outputs show political or racial bias
items.x: IVOs judge whether the safeguards are adequate, a step beyond checking compliance. "Acceptable" means the model's expected benefits outweigh its catastrophic risk, considering probability and size.

items.p: Who licenses IVOs?
o: The Under Secretary for AI Security
The developers they review, through an industry group
State attorneys general, each in their own state
The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
items.x: Applicants must show independence from the AI industry and submit a plan with their methods. The Under Secretary must revoke a license if, for example, the IVO's methods become obsolete or its independence is compromised.

items.p: Does IVO review cover models a lab only uses internally?
o: Yes. Internal use is covered too
No. Only publicly released models are covered
It covers them if the lab opts in, as a voluntary add-on
Internal models get reviewed once they're released, not before
items.x: Dan Parshall of the Canary Institute says including internal use "matters a lot, since the most capable models at any moment are the ones running inside the labs." Both outside IVO review and emergency orders reach internal use as well as released models.

items.p: How often must an IVO send an assessment report?
o: At least every 6 months, or more often if needed
Once, before the model is first released to the public
Every 5 years
Only when asked by Congress
items.x: Reports go to the Under Secretary and the developer at the same time. The Under Secretary can also order ad hoc assessments, for example after an incident.

items.p: What must an IVO do if it finds a model poses an imminent catastrophic risk?
o: Refer it to the Secretary of Commerce within 72 hours
Shut the model down itself
Notify the developer and give it 30 days to fix the problem
Wait and include it in the next scheduled assessment report
items.x: IVOs can't halt models themselves. They escalate to the Secretary, who decides whether to issue an emergency order.

items.p: Under the FRONTIER Act, put the review cycle between a developer and its independent verification organization (IVO) in order.
items: The IVO sends its assessment report
The developer describes its fixes within 14 days
The IVO says whether the fixes are adequate within 7 days
The developer files a post-assessment report with the Under Secretary within 30 days
items.x: The cycle forces a written record of what the IVO asked for and whether the developer did it. The full record goes to the Under Secretary. Within the same 30 days, the developer also publishes a redacted copy of the assessment report, which goes to the Attorney General and opted-in state attorneys general too.

items.p: Can an IVO be sued if a model it reviewed causes a catastrophe?
o: Only for willful misconduct causing death or serious injury, by clear and convincing proof
Yes, by anyone for any harm the model causes, under ordinary negligence rules
Never, under any circumstances, however serious the harm
Only by the developer that hired it
items.x: Licensed IVOs get broad immunity. The one exception is a federal claim for willful misconduct causing death or serious physical injury, and acting in line with the rules counts as no willful misconduct.

items.p: Who reports annually on whether the IVO market is working?
o: The Government Accountability Office (GAO)
The developers
The White House Office of Science and Technology Policy
The IVOs themselves, through a joint industry report
items.x: GAO, Congress's watchdog, reports each year on how many IVOs exist, whether they can meet demand and whether they're truly independent of the industry.

items.p: An IVO's license is at risk if a model it verified fails anyway. When is it protected?
o: When it flagged the problem and proposed adequate fixes the developer didn't make
When the model had passed its most recent scheduled assessment
When the failure happened overseas, outside United States jurisdiction
It's never protected
items.x: That rule gives IVOs a reason to put problems on the record rather than sign off quietly.

items.p: Why does Americans for Responsible Innovation (ARI) worry about the timing of IVO review?
o: Preemption is immediate; IVOs may take years
IVO licenses expire one year after they're issued
IVOs could only review open-source models, not closed ones
The bill bars any IVO from starting work until 2030
items.x: ARI president Brad Carson said the bill's preemption "would be effective immediately," while its private assurance market "will take years to set up." Very large developers don't have to hire an IVO until a year after the first one is licensed, while the limits on state law apply once the bill is enacted.

units.title: Emergency orders
units.desc: The government's power to halt a model.

items.p: Who can order a lab to suspend or restrict a frontier model?
o: The Secretary of Commerce
The Under Secretary, without the Secretary
Any licensed IVO, on its own authority
Any state attorney general, for models used in that state
items.x: The Secretary must consult the Under Secretary but holds final authority. An order can cover development, deployment or internal use, in whole or in part.

items.p: Match each type of order to how long it lasts.
pairs: Another 90 days, with a fresh finding each time
items.x: Provisional orders let the Secretary act fast on a preliminary determination. Final orders require a full written finding, and every renewal needs a new one based on current facts.

items.p: Before issuing a provisional order, what must the Secretary usually give the lab?
o: Notice and a chance to fix the problem and be heard
Nothing
A court order
Congressional approval
items.x: The Secretary can skip notice only by finding in writing that the risk is too imminent, and must then give the lab a chance to fix the problem right after.

items.p: Does an emergency order cover a fine-tuned copy of the model?
o: Yes, unless the order says otherwise, plus models trained largely on its outputs
No, only the exact model the order names, not any modified copies
Yes, but models trained on its outputs fall outside the order
Copies are covered once the Secretary names them in a separate order
items.x: Orders also bind affiliates, successors and anyone knowingly working with the developer, which keeps a lab from dodging an order by moving the model.

items.p: What can someone face for willfully violating an emergency order?
o: Up to a $1 million fine per violation and 10 years in prison
Only a warning letter from the Secretary of Commerce
Up to 6 months in prison and a $5,000 fine
A $500 fine per violation, with no prison time
items.x: That's the criminal penalty. Separately, anyone bound by an order who violates it faces civil penalties of up to $10 million per violation, with each day counting separately.

items.p: Under the FRONTIER Act, a lab contests an emergency order from the Secretary. Put the steps in order.
items: The Secretary serves a provisional order
The lab applies for an expedited hearing within 10 days
The Secretary issues a final order
The lab sues in federal district court in D.C.
items.x: Courts can't review a provisional order until a final order exists. Then the case goes only to the federal district court in D.C., which must move fast.

items.p: Which congressional committees get notice within 3 days of an emergency order?
o: Senate Commerce, House Energy and Commerce, and both Judiciary Committees
Only the House and Senate Intelligence Committees, in a closed classified briefing
The House and Senate Armed Services Committees
The House and Senate Appropriations Committees
items.x: The Secretary also reports semiannually on every order and its outcome. Notices can include a classified annex.

items.p: What does the bill's exclusivity clause do?
o: Makes this the only federal way to halt a model over imminent catastrophic risk
Gives the Commerce Department exclusive legal rights over every frontier model built in the U.S.
Bars states from writing their own catastrophic-risk rules for frontier developers
Gives IVOs the sole right to review frontier models for catastrophic risk
items.x: Any other attempt by the executive branch to halt a frontier model on those grounds is unenforceable unless a later law expressly refers to this section. Dan Parshall of the Canary Institute reads it as Congress "trying to wrest back some control from the Executive branch." It also means other emergency powers can't be used for this purpose. The bill’s limits on state laws are in a separate section.

items.p: A lab sues over a final order. Does the order stop applying while the case goes on?
o: No, unless the court orders a stay
Yes, the order is always paused until the case ends
Only if the lab posts bond
Yes, for 30 days while the court reviews the order
items.x: The court can set the order aside only if it's arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion or otherwise unlawful, a deferential standard. Claims that the law itself is unconstitutional can still be brought.

items.p: Which three areas would states be barred from adding new rules on?
o: Catastrophic-risk transparency, audits and incident reports
Children's online safety, personal data privacy and consumer protection
Election deepfakes, hiring algorithms, and housing and lending decisions
All AI regulation of any kind, from chatbots to self-driving cars
items.x: Section 9 blocks states from imposing new substantive obligations on AI developers in those three "covered subject areas," all tied to catastrophic risk.

items.p: Does the preemption clause reach only companies over the 10^26 threshold?
o: No, every AI developer
Yes, only frontier developers
Only very large developers
Only foreign AI developers
items.x: The federal duties apply only above the compute line, but the limit on states covers any AI developer's catastrophic-risk transparency, auditing and incident reporting. Section 9 defines an AI developer as any entity that builds, trains or owns an AI model, so states couldn't add rules in these areas even for developers the federal duties don't reach.

items.p: Name one kind of AI law a state could still pass under the bill.
o: Pass a law protecting minors from harmful AI chatbot content
Require AI developers to report catastrophic-risk incidents to the state
Require third-party audits of developers' catastrophic-risk safeguards
Require developers to publish their catastrophic-risk testing results
items.x: Protecting minors is one of four carve-outs, along with generally applicable laws, rules on how deployers and users use AI, and rules for state agencies' own AI use. The other three options fall in the covered subject areas.

items.p: Which existing state laws' frontier provisions would the preemption clause most directly hit?
o: California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act
Colorado’s 2026 automated decision-making law (SB 26-189)
Illinois's Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA)
Tennessee's ELVIS Act on AI voice cloning
items.x: Both require frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and report incidents, which falls in the covered areas. The sponsors pitch the bill as "a single, clear national standard" (Trahan's words) in place of a state patchwork. Critics such as ARI say state rules would end immediately while the federal system takes years to build.

items.p: How do state attorneys general fit into the federal scheme?
o: They can opt in to receive reports and sue to enforce federal rules
They're shut out entirely
They run the IVO licensing
They can veto any emergency order issued against a lab based in their state
items.x: This keeps a role for states in enforcement. In September 2026, 26 state attorneys general led by New York's Letitia James wrote to Congress asking for full state enforcement authority and no preemption, though their letter didn't name this bill.

news.h: 26 state attorneys general ask Congress to regulate frontier AI without preempting the states

items.p: What's the main objection from groups like Americans for Responsible Innovation?
o: Preemption ends state rules before the federal system is running
The bill is too weak on kids' safety
The bill would ban the release of open-source AI models
The bill's fees would push small AI startups out of the market
items.x: ARI president Brad Carson said the preemption clause leaves "a serious hole in regulatory oversight of AI models." ARI also noted there's no sunset on the preemption and that the bill leaves the decision to release risky models with developers.

items.p: What structural weakness has one critic flagged in how the bill sets up its new Under Secretary?
o: No Senate confirmation for the Under Secretary, and no appropriations
It creates too many new Senate-confirmed posts across the Commerce Department
The Under Secretary could halt models without the Secretary's sign-off
The office would sit in the FTC, away from Commerce's technical staff
items.x: This is a point Dan Parshall of the Canary Institute raised. The Under Secretary is appointed by the Secretary of Commerce, and the text funds only the registration system, through fees. Parshall also noted the bill has no severability clause and drops the whistleblower protections in the Great American AI Act discussion draft it grew out of.

items.p: Why did OpenAI's statement on the bill matter?
o: A top lab said it "can support" the IVO requirement
OpenAI threatened to move out of the U.S. if the bill passed
OpenAI endorsed the whole bill, including preemption
OpenAI came out against the IVO requirement
items.x: OpenAI's Chris Lehane told reporters on September 15, 2026 that the company "can support" the IVO requirement, though a spokesperson said OpenAI hadn't endorsed the whole bill. Outside industry, Foundation for American Innovation research fellow Daniel King called it "Congress's best AI bill yet," and the Institute for Law & AI's Charlie Bullock called it "by far the best AI safety bill ever introduced" in a statement released by Rep. Trahan's office.

items.p: What's the biggest obstacle to the bill passing this Congress?
o: The Energy and Commerce chair doesn't want to rush it
It already passed both chambers and was vetoed by the President
The Senate passed a rival version that House leaders reject
Its two lead sponsors are both in the minority party
items.x: Chairman Brett Guthrie said on September 16, 2026, "I'm not going to say that the bill is going to move," and that he wouldn't want to act quickly in a lame duck session. As of October 19, 2026, congress.gov showed no committee action. Any bill not passed by January 3, 2027 dies with the 119th Congress and would have to be reintroduced.

news.h: Energy and Commerce chair Brett Guthrie won't commit to moving the FRONTIER Act and warns against rushing it in the lame duck

items.p: How does the Senate's Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune draft reportedly differ from the FRONTIER Act?
o: It relies on a legal duty of care
It has nothing about preemption of state laws
It creates a new independent AI agency outside the Commerce Department
It would cover AI developers of every size
items.x: No Senate text had been made public as of mid-October 2026, so these details come from Reuters' September 11 report citing Senate aides, which said the draft would also preempt some state laws. When Cruz blocked a separate Democratic AI safety bill on September 29, he objected to its "unbounded discretion" for the federal government and suggested approaches "like involving independent judges." Any final deal would need to reconcile the two designs.
